title: Scars, a Parasternal Heave and a Quiet Diastolic Murmur After Childhood Surgery

blocks.text: Scars, a Parasternal Heave and a Quiet Diastolic Murmur After Childhood Surgery

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-40 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645); DVLA, Congenital heart disease and driving (page updated 9 September 2026) · Related AMaC: AMaC repaired tetralogy of Fallot, ventricular septal defect and Eisenmenger syndrome stations; this one tests pulmonary regurgitation and a near-faint after repair
The patient is a man of 36, a joiner. He had heart surgery as a child and attends for review. Please examine his cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A man with two chest scars, a right ventricular heave and a soft diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge has repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation. The marks come from separating it from aortic regurgitation, and from acting on a report of near-fainting.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates call a quiet low-pitched diastolic murmur aortic regurgitation and look for a collapsing pulse. Pass: heave, single second sound, no collapsing pulse, scars. Fail: aortic regurgitation, and routine review after near-fainting.

rows: He looks well. Check colour and hands, both radial pulses and both arm blood pressures, then the neck and the scars.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; both pulses; blood pressure; neck veins; scars.
Feel for the apex and a heave, then listen at the left sternal edge in held expiry and inspiration.
"I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles."
Apex; heave; thrill; second sound; murmurs in inspiration; lung bases; liver edge; ankles; cover him.
Name the lesion, the late problem and what decides intervention, and say what to do about near-fainting.
"This is repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation and right ventricular dilatation. He needs urgent review for the near-fainting."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; tests; urgent rhythm assessment; follow-up; thank him.
Starts without consent; presses hard on the chest; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone and stops if he is breathless.
Disorganised; omits the scars, the second radial pulse or the left sternal edge.
Looks at hands, colour and scars, feels both radial pulses, checks blood pressure, palpates for a heave, listens, then checks bases and ankles.
Also checks blood pressure in both arms and the liver edge.
Reports cyanosis, clubbing or a collapsing pulse that are absent.
Finds a sternotomy scar, a left thoracotomy scar, a weak left radial pulse, a heave, a single second sound and a diastolic murmur.
Also finds the murmur louder in inspiration and a soft systolic murmur, with blood pressure lower in the left arm.
Calls it aortic regurgitation, or a ventricular septal defect.
Repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation.
Also names the four original defects and separates the murmur from aortic regurgitation, which has a collapsing pulse.
Names right ventricular dilatation, arrhythmia and sudden death, and heart failure; asks for ECG, echo, cardiac magnetic resonance and exercise testing.
Also names residual outflow obstruction and a ventricular septal patch leak, and electrophysiological evaluation.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): calls him well and arranges routine review after he reports near-fainting.
Asks for same-day ECG and urgent cardiology review for a possible arrhythmia, and says follow-up stays with a specialist unit.

Also explains that valve replacement rests on symptoms and several criteria, with progressive right ventricular dilatation (RVESVi 80, RVEDVi 160 mL/m²) only one of them, and asks about driving: advise (as clinical advice, not DVLA wording) no driving until assessed, and say a car driver tells DVLA if symptoms affect safe driving.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: well; respiratory rate 14; pulse 76 regular, left radial weaker than right; blood pressure 124/74 right arm, 104/66 left arm; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. No cyanosis, no clubbing. Midline sternotomy scar and a left thoracotomy scar. JVP not raised. Apex not displaced; sustained left parasternal heave. Second sound single. Soft ejection systolic murmur and an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder in inspiration. No collapsing pulse. Lung bases clear. No oedema.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B, R3) Two scars, weak left radial pulse, left parasternal heave, single second sound, early diastolic murmur louder in inspiration, no collapsing pulse. 2. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation. 3. What were the original defects? (D, R4) Ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy. 4. What are the late problems? (E, R5) Right ventricular dilatation, arrhythmia, sudden death, heart failure, residual lesions. 5. He says he nearly fainted last week playing football; what do you do? (E, R6) Same-day ECG and urgent cardiology review for arrhythmia; no driving until assessed (clinical advice, not DVLA wording).

Curveballs: He asks about valve replacement: recommended for symptomatic severe pulmonary regurgitation; considered in an asymptomatic patient when criteria such as progressive right ventricular dilatation, falling exercise capacity or falling right ventricular function are met; decided in a specialist unit. He asks if he can keep driving: not until assessed (clinical advice, not DVLA wording). A car (Group 1) driver must tell DVLA if symptoms affect safe driving; a bus or lorry (Group 2) driver must always tell DVLA. He asks about children: congenital team review.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Checks both radial pulses and blood pressure in both arms (A)
Palpates for a left parasternal heave and listens at the left sternal edge (A)
Finds both scars and a weak left radial pulse (B)
Finds a single second sound and a diastolic murmur with no collapsing pulse (B)
Names repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation (D)
Names the four original defects (D)
Lists right ventricular dilatation, arrhythmia and sudden death (E)
Asks for same-day ECG and urgent cardiology review for near-fainting (E)
Covers him, cleans hands and thanks him (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the aortic area only.) [R2 Fail] Cyanosis and a collapsing pulse. [R3 Fail] Aortic regurgitation. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] He nearly fainted? Routine review in a year. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, as near-fainting after tetralogy repair may be a ventricular arrhythmia. No consent, the scars and the left sternal edge skipped, and the lesion misnamed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, colour, scars, both radial pulses, blood pressure, neck veins; heave; left sternal edge in inspiration; bases and ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He has a sternotomy and a left thoracotomy scar, a weak left radial pulse, a heave, a single second sound and a diastolic murmur, with no collapsing pulse. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Right ventricular dilatation, arrhythmia, sudden death and heart failure. ECG, echo, cardiac MRI and exercise test. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: He nearly fainted last week. What do you do?
CANDIDATE: A same-day ECG and urgent cardiology review for an arrhythmia; follow-up stays in a specialist unit. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not give the four defects, the outflow obstruction, the volume thresholds or driving.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, may I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll stop if you're breathless. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, both radial pulses, blood pressure in both arms, neck veins; heave; left sternal edge; liver edge; ankles.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: The diastolic murmur is louder in inspiration, there is a soft systolic murmur, and blood pressure is lower in the left arm. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?

CANDIDATE: Repaired tetralogy of Fallot: a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right outflow obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy. Not aortic regurgitation, as the pulse is not collapsing. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Also residual outflow obstruction and a patch leak. Electrophysiological evaluation if sudden-death risk factors are present. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: He nearly fainted. Management?

CANDIDATE: Same-day ECG and urgent review. Valve replacement is recommended for symptomatic severe regurgitation; if asymptomatic it is considered when one criterion is met, such as progressive right ventricular dilatation to an end-systolic volume index of 80 or end-diastolic 160 mL/m² or more on repeated measurements, falling exercise capacity, falling right ventricular function or worsening tricuspid regurgitation. The specialist unit decides. Does he drive? I would advise you not to drive until assessed (that is clinical advice, not DVLA wording), and DVLA must be told if symptoms affect safe driving. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, both arm pressures, the four defects, the patch leak, the criteria for valve replacement and driving.
R2: Listening only in the aortic area. The diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation is at the left sternal edge.
R4: Calling it aortic regurgitation. The pulse is not collapsing, and the heave points to the right ventricle.
R5: Naming heart failure alone. Arrhythmia and sudden death are the late dangers.
R6: Arranging routine review after near-fainting. A possible ventricular arrhythmia needs assessment now.
"May I listen at the left sternal edge in held inspiration?"
"There is a heave and no collapsing pulse, so I'd say right-sided, not aortic regurgitation."
"Near-fainting needs an urgent rhythm assessment; may I say what I'd do?"

Repaired tetralogy of Fallot: a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy. Late pulmonary regurgitation dilates the right ventricle and brings arrhythmia and sudden death.

ESC 2020: valve replacement is recommended (Class I) in symptomatic patients with severe pulmonary regurgitation and/or at least moderate outflow obstruction. In asymptomatic patients with severe regurgitation and/or obstruction it should be considered (Class IIa) when one of these is present: falling objective exercise capacity; progressive right ventricular dilatation to an end-systolic volume index of 80 mL/m² or more and/or end-diastolic volume index of 160 mL/m² or more, confirmed on repeated measurements; progression of tricuspid regurgitation to at least moderate; progressive right ventricular systolic dysfunction; outflow obstruction with right ventricular systolic pressure above 80 mmHg. The volumes are interpreted with the clinical picture, not applied in isolation. Electrophysiological evaluation should be considered (Class IIa) for sudden-death risk stratification with additional risk factors. Follow-up is lifelong in a specialised adult congenital unit, with regular cardiac magnetic resonance.

DVLA (page updated 9 September 2026): car and motorcycle (Group 1) drivers must tell DVLA if congenital heart disease causes symptoms that affect safe driving; bus, coach and lorry (Group 2) drivers must tell DVLA if they have congenital heart disease.
THINK: Scars, heave, single S2, diastolic murmur: repaired Fallot.
SAY: "Pulmonary regurgitation after repair of tetralogy of Fallot."
DO: Both radial pulses; heave; left sternal edge in inspiration.
NUMBERS: RVESVi 80 / RVEDVi 160 mL/m²: one criterion among several, on repeated measurements (ESC 2020).
TRAP: Aortic regurgitation; routine review after near-fainting.
FINISH: ECG today, urgent review, specialist unit follow-up.

European Society of Cardiology. 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaa554 Supports: criteria for pulmonary valve replacement, electrophysiological evaluation and specialised follow-up.
DVLA. Congenital heart disease and driving (page updated 9 September 2026). https://www.gov.uk/congenital-heart-disease-and-driving Supports: When to tell DVLA, Group 1 and Group 2.
